title: Do You Have To Lie To Be A Good Teacher?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts an unsettling after-class conversation in which a student and her friends described widespread teacher dishonesty — broken promises, unenforced threats, and praise that didn't match reality. He connects this directly to SCM's emphasis on transparency and consistency, arguing that a reputation for straight-shooting builds trust, loyalty, and authority, while perceived dishonesty erodes a teacher's standing. He clarifies that honesty with students doesn't require sharing private life details or political opinions, offering scripted responses for both. The piece closes on the idea that being the rare consistently truthful teacher earns outsized respect and attention from students who have grown jaded by broken promises elsewhere.
points: Recounts students describing widespread teacher dishonesty around broken promises, unenforced rules, and inflated praise.
Identifies three recurring student complaints: promises never kept, threats/rules never followed through, and praise that doesn't match reality.
Argues perceived dishonesty causes students to discount what a teacher says and lowers their opinion of the teacher's leadership.
Clarifies that honesty with students does not require disclosing private life details or personal political views, offering scripted deflections.
Concludes that being the rare consistently truthful teacher earns outsized trust, attention, and respect from students.
quotes: Several of her friends, who’d been listening to our conversation, chimed in with their own stories.
Because, being a straight-shooter is an easy and remarkably effective way to build trust, loyalty, and authority.
If your students believe you’re being untruthful or misleading, then they put far less stock what you say.
It’s not appropriate for me as your teacher to share that with you.

You see, when you’re the one teacher who tells it like it is , does what they say they’re going to do, and protects their freedom to form their own thoughts, ideas, and opinions, they go overboard in their appreciation for you.
